study.title: Jeremiah 15 - Unavoidable Judgment and Preservation of the Prophet
study.overview: In this chapter, the LORD responds to Jeremiah's intercession with a hard sentence on Judah: not even the mediation of Moses and Samuel would change the decree, because the sin of the people has matured for judgment. Destruction is described in strong images of death, sword, famine, captivity, abandonment and mourning. In the midst of this severe word, Jeremiah also reveals his own anguish: he suffers because he is rejected and insulted by speaking in the name of God. The LORD corrects him, but he also restores and reaffirms his protection, promising that he will stand against his enemies.

outline.title: Rejected intercession and unavoidable judgment
outline.explanation: The LORD declares that the intercession of the greatest known mediators would not change the decision against Judah. The people are already handed over to various deaths, war, famine and captivity. The mention of Manasseh shows that the national guilt accumulated in Jerusalem weighs on the present.

outline.title: Jerusalem without comfort and without heirs
outline.explanation: God describes the city as one who will not find compassion, for abandonment is the result of having departed from the Lord. The picture includes widows, devastation at noon and the image of a once fertile and now humiliated woman, with survivors handed over to the sword.

outline.title: The pain of the prophet and the certainty of punishment
outline.explanation: Jeremiah laments his vocation of conflict and his rejection by all. The LORD responds that he will deliver him for good, but also states that the enemy of the north is stronger than Judah; because of sins, wealth, and treasuries will be plundered, and the people will be taken to an unknown land.

outline.title: Prayer of Jeremiah, divine correction and promise of protection
outline.explanation: Jeremiah appeals to God on the basis of his sincerity and suffering he carries because of the Lord. God calls him back to faithfulness, promises to do so as a divine mouth if he distinguishes the precious from the vible, and assures him of protection: as a bronze wall, he will not be overcome, and will be rescued from the evil and the terrible.

study.context: The notes provided highlight that this chapter responds to Jeremiah's previous prayer and shows a decisive moment in his relationship with the Lord. Tyndale notes that Moses and Samuel were known for their effective intercession in the past, but here not this holds the judgment. Matthew Henry reads the chapter as the ratification of the sentence against the people, despite the prophet's prayers, and also as the account of Jeremiah's inner discouragement. Adam Clarke highlights the intensity of the announcement of punishment, the variety of punishments, and then the reaffirmation of divine protection to the prophet. The text therefore unites national judgment and personal care.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that God's mercy does not cancel his holiness or postpones judgment indefinitely when rebellion matures. The intercession is real and precious, but does not manipulate God against his righteousness. The memory of Manasseh shows moral continuity: sin can leave lasting consequences on the community. At the same time, Jeremiah is preserved as a faithful prophet; God does not abandon him in the midst of opposition, but rather corrects and strengthens him. There is here an important biblical tension: the messenger suffers from the word he announces, but God himself supports the messenger so that he may remain before him and keep speaking faithfully. The promise to be "like my mouth" suggests that prophetic authority depends on continuous obedience, not just the initial call.

scholarViews.insight: The intercession of Moses and Samuel, effective at other times in Israel's history, would no longer suffice here; judgment had become inevitable.
Even with the prophet's prayers, God ratifies the sentence against the people and abandons Judah to ruin.
The expression of the verse describes different forms of punishment to death, sword, famine, and captivity - according to the gravity of sin.

questions: Why does the text emphasize that not even Moses and Samuel would change the divine decree against Judah?
What does the memory of Manasseh teach about personal sin and collective consequences?
How can Jeremiah mourn his pain and still continue to be called by God to speak in his name?
study.practice: This chapter calls on the reader to take the holiness of God seriously and perseverance in faithfulness. A concrete application is to examine whether there are stubborn areas of resistance to divine correction and respond with repentance before hardening produces greater loss. It also teaches not to measure God's call by the absence of opposition: Jeremiah was rejected, but remained sustained. In practice, this encourages to speak truth faithfully, even when it is unpopular, and to seek comfort in God when Christian service brings tiredness, misunderstanding or isolation.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not clarify in detail some poetic elements of the chapter, such as the image of the "iron of the north" and certain figurative expressions about grief and devastation. There is also not enough base notes in the notes to accurately affirm the complete historical context beyond what the text itself and the commentators mention. Therefore, more specific readings about dates, geography or exact identification of enemies have been avoided.
